Cloning the factor zoo: replicating Fama-French, Hou-Xue-Zhang, and Stambaugh-Yuan

Author

JKP data team

Published

May 25, 2026

Overview

We now replicate the standard factor zoo inside the JKP database. The ap_factors_monthly.parquet output produced by jkp build contains country-level monthly returns for:

  • FF3 (Fama–French 3): smb_ff3, hml
  • FF5 (Fama–French 5): smb_ff5, hml, rmw, cma
  • UMD (FF momentum): umd_ff
  • HXZ q-factors: me_hxz, ia_hxz, roe_hxz
  • MP (Stambaugh–Yuan mispricing): smb_mispricing, mispricing_mgmt, mispricing_perf

This document benchmarks the USA replications against the original / WRDS-distributed series stored in factor_comparison/Reference_data/.

Data & method

This document benchmarks the US replications against the original / WRDS-distributed series. For the international panels, we have made discretionary choices in the construction of each factor that try to emulate the spirit of the original US procedure (e.g., NYSE-style size breakpoints replaced with country-specific breakpoints, accounting conventions adapted to each excntry’s Compustat coverage, etc.).

Factor construction is implemented in ap_factor_model_data in src/jkp/data/aux_functions.py, which unifies the per-model builders (FF3, FF5, UMD, HXZ q-factors, Stambaugh–Yuan mispricing) into the ap_factors_monthly.parquet and ap_factors_daily.parquet outputs under data/interim/.

Some drift from the published references is expected: Compustat is updated continuously, so accounting variables for older fiscal years get revised over time, which feeds into any sort that conditions on book equity, profitability, or investment. To reduce this vintage drift for the Stambaugh–Yuan factors, the official mispricing-factor replication package was run during the development of the Python code, so the JKP MP series and the reference series are constructed from roughly the same Compustat snapshot.

What the factors are

  • FF3 (Fama–French 1992, 1993) — smb_ff3 is the size factor (small-minus-big) from a 2×3 size × book-to-market sort; hml is the value factor (high-minus-low book-to-market) from the same sort.
  • FF5 (Fama–French 2015) — built from a 2×3 size × {B/M, profitability, investment} sort. smb_ff5 is the redefined size factor (averaged across the three sorts); hml is value; rmw is robust-minus-weak operating profitability; cma is conservative-minus-aggressive investment.
  • UMD (Carhart 1997 / Fama–French momentum) — umd_ff is the momentum factor: winners-minus-losers based on prior 12-month return skipping the most recent month, within size buckets.
  • HXZ q-factors (Hou, Xue, and Zhang 2015) — me_hxz (size), ia_hxz (investment), roe_hxz (profitability), constructed from a 2×3×3 triple sort on size, investment-to-assets, and return on equity.
  • MP (Stambaugh and Yuan 2017) — mispricing_mgmt and mispricing_perf are long–short composite mispricing factors built from 11 anomalies grouped into a “management” cluster and a “performance” cluster; smb_mispricing is the size factor from the same triple sort.

Sample window — 1970 onwards. We restrict the comparison sample to 1970 onwards because parts of the FF construction in the 1960s rely on accounting data that did not yet come from Compustat. Including the 1960s would benchmark our Compustat-based replication against a reference series built on a different accounting source.

Reasons for divergence

  • Differences in CRSP Legacy vs CRSP V2. Historical fields — delisting returns, share codes, exchange codes — differ between the two CRSP products, producing vintage drift in pre-2000 data.

  • Undisclosed filters in the papers. Source papers omit secondary screens (e.g., stale prices, thin trading, dual-class consolidation, fiscal-year changers, share-class screens, price floors) that the reference WRDS implementations carry as undocumented adjustments. Exact parity is not achievable without the original construction code.

Conclusion

Residual gaps trace to data-vintage drift and undisclosed construction choices — both outside the scope of an external replication. The JKP factor series are suitable for research use as drop-in replacements for the published US factors. The added value of this replication is that we publish FF, HXZ, and Stambaugh–Yuan style factors for the rest of the country panel using the same methodology, and these international factors can likewise be used for research where no public benchmark exists. The full construction pipeline is open-source and fully replicable end-to-end from raw WRDS data.

Appendix: Replication of daily data

Show daily replication tables

Daily factor returns are mechanically noisier than monthly returns: small differences in universe filters, delisting handling, or trading calendars compound day-by-day, so day-level correlations are typically lower and day-level Mean / StD figures more dispersed than at the monthly frequency.
